chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 191 to 200, Ammuvanar's neythal decade of the bangle: the conch shell of the shore sawn into bangles, which the man sees on the girl he cannot reach, the friend weighs as a lover's gift and as a reason to marry, and the woman reads as a gauge that loosens when the lord of the shore leaves and tightens when he returns.

191.reading: The man says that the girl with bangles of sea conch on her long forearms, backwater flowers strung through her dark heavy hair and a fine leaf skirt of the shore grove's njaazhal, harder to win than the nymphs of the mountain, has taken his heart that could not hold itself and hidden it away.
191.nuance: Everything she wears is of the shore, conch at the wrist, backwater flowers in the hair, a skirt of njaazhal leaves, and only the measure of her is brought down from the mountain: she is a fisher girl, yet rarer than its goddesses. The theft runs the other way from the decade's usual loss: here it is the man's heart, நிறையரு (past holding), that is carried off and hidden.

thinai_evidence.note: conch, backwater flowers and njaazhal of the shore grove dress her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the man describes the girl and speaks of his own heart, so he is taken to speak to it or to his companion

192.reading: The woman tells her friend that when the lord of the cold roaring ford, where the sea rises and thunders so the shores seem to whirl and running boats are driven out, went away, her bangles slipped loose, and now they have grown tight again.
192.nuance: The two verbs stand side by side with no clause between them, நெகிழ்ந்தன (loosened) then வீங்கின (swelled, grew tight): the bangle is a gauge that reads both ways, and the second verb, ending in the exclamation மாதோ, reports his return without naming it. Whether வீங்கின means the arm has filled out again with his coming is the reading the sense turns on.

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring sea, the boats and the lord of the ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; she says தோழி and என் வளை

193.reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore, where the right-whorled conch ploughs the long sand of the bank and pearls with shining rays glitter so the darkness is gone, whether the white bangles from the dashing sea that he has given are good, then.
193.nuance: The question நல்லவோ தாமே can be plain or barbed: on a shore where conch and pearl lie about lighting the dark, a gift of shell bangles is a small thing, and the friend may be asking whether such gifts can stand in for the marriage he delays. The sense turns on the tone, which four lines do not fix.

thinai_evidence.note: conch and pearl on the sea bank

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the hero is addressed as கொண்க and asked about the bangles he gave, which suits the friend weighing a lover's gift

194.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore that they have seen the young girl with bright bracelets, with lovely bangles sawn from sea conch, and because her fine brow is today clouded with longing, the mother has suspected some wrong cause, and that is how the mother stands.
194.nuance: கொன் ஒன்று (some cause, in vain) is the whole of the mother's mistake in two words: she reads the girl's pallor as something other than love, the misreading that in longer poems brings the diviner and the veri rite, and the friend reports it to the man as the danger that only marriage will end.

thinai_evidence.note: conch sawn into bangles, and the shore lord addressed

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the hero is addressed as கொண்க and told of the girl and her mother, which is the friend's warning

195.reading: The man says that the dear young daughter of the sea lord, on whose shore fishermen sell the pearls born of the conch, has given him a grief that will not pass and stolen his sleep on his bed.
195.nuance: நல்கி, the verb of a patron's gift, is used for a sorrow, and the pearl that fishermen cry for sale sits beside the daughter no one may buy: a reader may hear in the pearl born of the conch the girl born of the chief, but the poem draws no second pair, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen selling pearls on the sea shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the man speaks of the girl as the sea lord's daughter, as one does to the friend whose help he needs

196.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool sea shore, where red prawns are caught in the clear backwater, that if he wants the girl with bright bangles cut from conch, rich heavy hair and fine bracelets, he should marry her and take her.
196.nuance: The condition is put coolly, வேண்டுதி யாயின் (if you want her), so the demand to marry comes as the only terms on offer; the prawns caught in the clear backwater may suggest a catch to be landed properly, but a single image makes no ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns of the backwater and the lord of the sea shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the hero is told வரைந்தனை கொண்மோ (marry and take her), the friend's demand

197.reading: The man says that the girl who stood bowed with her face hidden in her hair, her shining bangles jingling as she chased the crabs, will give him her lovely breast so that the lonely evening is gone.
197.nuance: Two moments are set against each other: the girl caught at a child's game, then bowing and hiding her face once she is seen, and the man's certainty that the same girl will ease his evening. Her shame (முகம்புதை, இறைஞ்சி) is the sign he reads as consent.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore crab and the lonely evening, neythal's hour

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the man speaks of what the girl will give எனக்கே, to his own heart or companion

198.reading: The friend says that they have seen the tall-shouldered noble man who stood asking about the small ford, in the shore grove where loose-budded flowers open and young girls with bangled forearms, white teeth and gentle smiles play.
198.nuance: A man of tall shoulders stops to ask about a small ford: the question is the pretext of the first approach, and the friend's கண்டிக்கும் (we have seen) says she has seen through it.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the small ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; யாமே (we) and the report of a man seen at the grove fit the friend telling the girl what she noticed

199.reading: The woman asks her friend to come with her and climb the sky-high long sand dune that the roaring waves beat at the great ford of the shore grove, and gaze without end at the land of the wave-dashed sea of him who loosened her close bangles.
199.nuance: She names him only by what he has done to her, செறிவளை நெகிழ்த்தோன் (he who loosened the close bangles), and the remedy she proposes is not to hide the sign but to climb the highest dune in view of all and look at his country, ஆனாது (without stopping).

thinai_evidence.note: parted, she can only gaze toward his land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; she says தோழி and names him by her loosened bangles

200.reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord with the golden chariot has now come, so that her shining bangles fit tight and her fine brow grows lovely; let her long eyes with their red lines ease, and let them laugh at the pallor that took her beauty.
200.nuance: The decade ends by reversing its token: the bangle that slipped is வீங்கு (swelling, tight) again, and the pallor that ruled her is turned into something to mock. பொலந்தேர் (the golden chariot) suggests he comes openly, in state, not by stealth.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord comes and the bangles tighten

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the girl is told her lover has come and invited to laugh with the speaker (நகுக நாமே)

links.note: The Kural man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Ainkurunuru man knows she is a shore girl and says she is harder to win than the mountain nymphs (வரையர மகளிரின் அரியள்).
links.teaches: The likeness to a goddess can carry two different fears: in the couplet it is bewilderment at what she is, in the shore poem it is despair of reaching her, so the divine comparison in akam measures distance as often as beauty.

links.note: Both have the woman of the shore say her bangles registered the lord's leaving (தணந்தமை ... உணர்ந்த வளை; பிரிந்தென நெகிழ்ந்தன); Ainkurunuru 192 adds that they have grown tight again (வீங்கின).
links.teaches: The Kural treats the bangle only as an early witness of separation, while the Ainkurunuru poem shows it registering his return as well, so the convention is a two-way gauge of the man's presence and not merely a sign of wasting.

links.note: Natrinai 282's friend, the hero within hearing, describes the slipping bangles, faded brow and the old diviner misreading the illness; Ainkurunuru 194's friend tells the hero directly that the mother has suspected a wrong cause (கொன் ஒன்று கடுத்தனள்).
links.teaches: Set beside Natrinai's full scene of pebbles and diviner, the Ainkurunuru friend's two words show the misread illness was familiar enough to be invoked in a half-line, and that in both its use is the same: to press the man to marry before a wrong cure exposes the girl.

links.note: Both men say the bangled girl has given them suffering, with the verb of a gift (துயரம் நல்கி; தந்தாள் ... துயர்); in the Kural the gift is the palmyra horse and the evening's pain, in Ainkurunuru 195 a grief that will not pass and lost sleep.
links.teaches: Read together they show the stages of the same plea to the friend: the Ainkurunuru man stops at sleeplessness, and the couplet shows where his complaint goes next if no one answers it, to the threat of riding the palmyra horse.

links.note: In Akananuru 380 the shore lord leaves his chariot far off and asks the girls the name of their town; in Ainkurunuru 198 the tall-shouldered man stands asking about the small ford where girls play.
links.teaches: The question about a ford or a town is the fixed first move of the shore courtship: Ainkurunuru 198 catches it as it is asked, and Akananuru 380 shows the friend later reading the same pretext as the start of a suit that ends in his shame and her consent.

links.note: In the Kural the slipping bangles spread the news (தூற்றா) that the lord of the shore has left; in Ainkurunuru 199 the woman names him by the bangles he loosened and asks to climb the high dune to gaze at his land.
links.teaches: The couplet's woman fears her bangles will publish the loss to the town, while the Ainkurunuru woman makes the loss her name for him and climbs where all can see her looking, so the same token can be suffered as exposure or claimed in the open.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
194 line 2 and 198 line 4 read கண்டிக்கும், with a doubled க், where the refrain elsewhere in Ainkurunuru is கண்டிகும் (we have seen); likely a misprint.
192 line 1 கோடுபுலம் கொட்ப is obscure (கோடு as shore or as conch); the sense of the opening scene is taken loosely.
195 line 4 படலின் பாயல் is unclear (படல் as lying down or as a woven mat); the sense, his sleep on his bed, is not affected.
199 line 4 lacks the final full stop the other poems carry; no effect on the sense.
